summary: Frederik Bisbjerg, Deputy CEO and independent board member in insurance, explains pluralistic ignorance: group members privately disagree with something but stay silent because they assume everyone else agrees. He gives examples from corporate engineering teams, a gang, and Germans under Hitler, and argues that new employees' fresh views are often met with resistance for this reason. He recommends gentle, repeated conversations and one-on-one follow-up to draw colleagues out, and says the best organizations reward employees who speak their minds. The page also carries LinkedIn comments praising the article and a list of the author's other articles.
one_line: Frederik Bisbjerg explains how pluralistic ignorance silences employees in organizations and suggests gentle, repeated conversations to bring out their real views.
key_facts: Frederik Bisbjerg's article 'Dealing with pluralistic ignorance' was published on LinkedIn on Jun 16, 2017.
Frederik Bisbjerg is described as Deputy CEO | Independent Board Member | Shaping the Future of Insurance.
Pluralistic ignorance is when members of a crowd believe something is wrong but say nothing because they think everybody else believes it is right.
The article gives a corporate example in which a group of engineers sees a design is outdated but keeps quiet because they believe their peers think it is still the right design.
The article states that many Germans privately believed Hitler was a barbarian but pretended to support him because they falsely thought they were alone with their views.
The article describes pluralistic ignorance as 'peer pressure with added irony'.
Bisbjerg says he always welcomes 'fresh blood' into older organizations because new colleagues bring a fresh view on the world.
The article says new employees who present views on the organization often meet modest acceptance or even resistance.

Possible reasons for pluralistic ignorance listed in the article include fear for one's position, feeling lacking in skills to deal with 'the new', and wanting to follow what the leader does and says.
The article advises that removing pluralistic ignorance requires lots of talks done in a very gentle way.
The article suggests being blunt and repeatedly pointing out 'the elephant in the room' as an option.
Bisbjerg writes that colleagues will gradually open up if talks are followed up with one-on-one conversations promoting one's view.
Bisbjerg argues that the best colleagues speak their mind and the best organizations reward employees for doing so.
Bisbjerg attributes much of the silence to people's own insecurity and their desire to belong to a group and avoid expulsion from peer groups.
The article had 18 likes and 5 comments at the time of capture.
